1.pericope_label: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman. Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit. Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.

schools.summary: Ellicott canvasses what suggested the figure, tendrils in the room, the vine carved on the Temple doors, vineyards by moonlight, or the cup just drunk, inclines to the cup and then refuses to go further; he warns that the branch taken away means Christians in name rather than the unbelieving world, renders the last clause already are ye clean with the pronoun emphatic, and reads the pruning as the removal of whatever misdirects the energy of the spiritual life. Barnes prefers vine-dresser to husbandman, makes the point of the figure that all nourishment passes through the one stalk, and exposes the wordplay by which taketh away, cleanseth and clean share a stem. Robertson renders the phrase the vine the genuine, notes that Israel appeared as a vine on the Maccabean coinage, traces the word for branch to a root meaning to break, and ends with the remark that the clause about bearing more fruit is a good test for modern church members. Lightfoot sets the word true against Israel the vine, reports a rabbinic parallel drawn out to sixteen particulars which he thinks mostly forced, and argues that men are henceforth grafted into Christ rather than into the Jewish religion.

Gill dates the saying after the Supper, takes the figure chiefly of fruitfulness rather than lowliness, and distinguishes two sorts of branches, those with an historical faith who are in Christ by profession only, as whole churches bear the name without every member being in him. Calvin weighs whether the Greek makes Christ the plant or the planted ground, cites Cicero for the diminutive, and then declines to debate it, laying down instead the rule that a parable is taken in its general view rather than in every property, and finding three parts in this one: that no power of doing good is ours, that having root in him we are dressed by the Father, and that the barren are removed and burnt. He names the instrument of cleansing as the doctrine they had heard.

Clarke supposes vines seen on the road from Bethany to Gethsemane, notes that some manuscripts and several fathers add ye are the branches to the first verse, names the cases of the branch taken away as Judas, the unbelieving Jews and the apostatising disciples, and insists the second verb means pruned rather than purged, producing Horace paring his nails with a penknife for the usage. Wesley glosses true as most excellent, comparing the true bread, and observes that purity and fruitfulness help each other.

Henry finds humility in so low a comparison, that the Sun of righteousness should liken himself to a vine whose outside is unsightly as its antitype had no form nor comeliness; unfruitful trees are said to lie, but this vine will not deceive those who gather from it, as the wild gourds did.

debates.question: What suggested the figure of the vine?

positions.position: Vines seen on the road from Bethany to Gethsemane
The walk to Olivet, rather than the upper room or the Temple with its golden vine
Most probably the cup of the fruit of the vine just drunk, though the prompt may be some incident now unknown

outliers.claim: Argues that the word true marks a change of grafting stock, so that converts are henceforth planted into Christ and not into the Jewish religion, which is why the disciples at Antioch came to be called by another name than Jews

themes: I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
Now ye are clean through the word which I have spoken unto you.

4.pericope_label: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing. If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the command and the promise as cause and effect, so that the union is placed within reach of the will, holds that the denial of power apart from Christ has often been unduly pressed since the context limits it to the fruit-bearing of the Christian life and the New Testament plainly recognises moral power outside Christianity, and would render the last clause and they burn rather than are burned, the tenses looking back from the final judgment. Barnes keeps to dependence and its practical upshot, that good works are done in proportion as the dependence is felt, and points out that the word men is absent from the Greek, the verb being an impersonal they, the gathering being referred to angels. Robertson notes the aorist imperative, warns that blind complacency is a peril to the preacher, calls the later aorists timeless, and supplies the servants of the vine-dresser as the unnamed subject of the gathering. Lightfoot alone suspects a particular danger in view, apostasy out of the gospel back into Judaism, and finds the force of the withered branch in Ezekiel, where the Jewish commentators take it for the wild vine of the forest, unfruitful as the forest trees and fit only for burning.

Gill observes that the words are not if ye abide not, which Christ would not suppose of true disciples, and refers the case to Judas and to any who profess and then deny. Calvin hears reassurance rather than threat, since Christ did not begin the work of salvation to leave it unfinished, takes the denial of power absolutely against those who concede the words and then imagine a co-operating power of their own, and denies that any of the elect is ever dried up, assigning the withering to hypocrites who are green for a season.

Clarke turns the command into two duties, holding fast faith and a good conscience and continually receiving power to do good, reaches for parallels in a scripture of the Hindoos where the deity calls himself sacrifice, worship, fire and victim and in a line of Theophilus that God is not contained but is himself the place of all things, and refuses the evasion of a merely seeming union, since no one cuts off a branch that was never joined. Wesley is blunter still, that a man cast out of the vineyard was in it once.

Chrysostom presses the division of labour, that the Son contributes no less than the Father, since the Father prunes while the Son keeps them in himself, and that to be cast forth means simply losing the husbandman's care.

Augustine fixes on the asymmetry of the two abidings, since the branches contribute nothing to the vine and draw everything from it, so that both the abiding and the indwelling profit the disciples and not Christ; when a branch is cut off another may spring from the living root, while the severed branch cannot live apart from it; and he will not soften the conclusion, observing that the text does not say you can do little.

debates.question: Can a branch truly united to Christ be lost?

positions.position: Yes: a man cast out of the vineyard was in it once
Yes: no one cuts off a branch that was never joined, and a merely seeming union could suffer only a seeming excision
No: none of the elect is ever dried up, and the withering belongs to hypocrites green for a season
No: the words are not if ye abide not, and the case is that of professors who never had real connection

debates.question: How far does the denial of power apart from Christ reach?

positions.position: Absolutely, leaving nothing to us but what is imparted, since before we are in him we are dry and useless wood
Only to the fruit-bearing of the Christian life, since moral power outside Christianity is plainly recognised elsewhere

outliers.claim: Sets beside the saying a passage from a scripture of the Hindoos in which the deity declares himself the sacrifice, the worship, the fire and the victim, and asks whether such sentiments could come from any source but divine revelation

themes: Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.

7.pericope_label: If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you. Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples. As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love. If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and abide in his love. These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.

schools.summary: Ellicott thinks the verb about asking is probably imperative and makes the abiding of the words both the means of abiding in Christ and its proof; he objects that taking herein of what follows forces a conjunction which properly expresses purpose, and prefers to let it look back; he corrects continue to abide and insists my love means his love toward them rather than theirs to him; and he identifies the joy as Christ's own, lit by the mutual love of Father and Son, judging that those whose religion sheds no such light have learnt little of Christianity. Barnes restricts the promise about asking to the apostles and to others only so far as they share their spirit, recalling that iniquity regarded in the heart stops the ear of God, and distinguishes kind from degree in the comparison of loves. Robertson calls the command astounding and immediately conditions it, agrees that herein points both ways, makes the last verb become rather than be, notes the emphatic possessive in the love I have for you, and treats the closing clause as the consummation of a process.

Gill speaks of the word becoming engrafted, and agrees that continuance in Christ's affection does not hang on our observance, reading the promise as fuller discoveries of a love already held. Calvin says God lets his people hunger to train them to earnestness and denies that leave is given to frame wishes by our own fancy, since what the promise covers is the vital sap of the Spirit and not riches or honours; he brushes aside those who take the love of this passage for the eternal love of the Father toward the Son, saying they philosophise away from the subject, and warns that whoever asks how God loves him without looking through the Mediator enters a labyrinth with neither entrance nor exit; obedience he calls the effect of that love and not its cause.

Clarke reduces the promise to four steps and states the converse of the condition, that no sense of pardoning love survives without the obedience of faith; on the joy he takes the last word as filled to the brim like a vessel, says it was to drive wretchedness out of the world that Christ came into it, and notes that Bishop Pearce would construe the clause as my joy in you. Wesley observes that prayers are themselves a fruit of faith, calls discipleship at once the foundation and the height of Christianity, and puts the condition of abiding more sharply than the others, on these terms and no other.
Henry counts a fourfold love here and observes that the Son kept his place in it even when it pleased the Father to bruise him, so those God loves may despise the hatred of the world.

Chrysostom makes the promise an assurance, that if the Father's glory is bound up with their fruitfulness he will hardly despise his own glory, and likens a soul fainting near the end of its labours to a great ship foundering within sight of harbour, which gains nothing from the length of its voyage and only makes the loss heavier.

debates.question: Whose love is meant by abide in my love?

positions.position: His love toward the disciples, not their love to him
Not the eternal love of the Father toward the Son, which is to philosophise away from the subject, but love toward us seen in the Mediator

debates.question: Does obedience secure the love or follow from it?

positions.position: It is the effect and not the cause, so our security does not rest on ourselves
Continuance in his affection does not hang on our observance; the promise is of fuller discoveries of a love already held
On these terms and no other
The condition is not arbitrary, since keeping commandments is what love necessarily does

outliers.claim: Rejects the usual construction of herein, arguing that referring it to the words which follow forces the conjunction, which properly expresses purpose, so that the sense should run: in this granting of whatever you ask my Father is glorified, in order that you may bear much fruit

themes: If ye abide in me, and my words abide in you, ye shall ask what ye will, and it shall be done unto you.
Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.
As the Father hath loved me, so have I loved you: continue ye in my love.
If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and abide in his love.
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full.

12.pericope_label: This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you. Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends. Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you. Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that love to God is proved by love to men, so the two great commandments are really one, denies any conflict with the apostolic statement about dying for the ungodly since what is weighed here is the height of love rather than the worth of its object, lays stress on the pronoun in ye are my friends, and notes the irony that the word refused means bond-slave and was afterwards taken by the foremost apostles as their own favourite title. Barnes recalls Damon and Pythias as a rare case of a man dying for a friend and makes the rarity the point, since Christ died for enemies, and gives the reason for the change of title, that it is a condition of slavery not to be admitted to a master's counsels while friendship's privilege is to know his plans. Robertson notes that they are to keep on loving, quotes the phrase that self-sacrifice is the high-water mark of love, makes the obedience continued rather than spasmodic, and asks whether we are friends of Christ. Lightfoot supplies the sabbath blessing over a departing course of priests, which asked that brotherhood, love, peace and friendship be planted among them, observes that tradition had largely put the command out of use, and recalls that Abraham bore the name of friend first.

Gill makes this the principal command, to which every duty between Christians reduces, and refers the older condition of servants to the legal dispensation, where children differed nothing from servants under a spirit of bondage. Calvin denies the honour of friendship is earned by merit while keeping the condition intact, observes that God could have redeemed us by a word but judged it better not to spare his own Son, and takes the whole as proof of love, the heart of Christ laid open in the gospel, so none need climb above the clouds or search the deep for assurance.

Clarke passes on an old Latin story of the aged evangelist, carried into the assemblies and saying nothing but little children, love one another, who when asked why he always said the same thing answered that it is the Lord's commandment and doing that alone is enough. Wesley fires the sharpest sentence in the chapter at the condition attached to friendship, a thunderbolt for Antinomianism, and asks who dares say God's love does not at all depend on works.
Origen sets the servant who has the spirit of bondage against the friend, quoting the complaint in Malachi that a master should be feared, and noting that the servant does not know the master's will.

Augustine draws from the epistle that we ought in turn to lay down our lives for the brethren and finds the sacrament in the proverb about sitting at a ruler's table, that table being the one from which we take the body and blood of him who laid down his life; he calls the naming of friends great condescension, since a man cannot be even a good servant without doing his lord's commands and the marks of a good servant are made the marks of a friend; and he raises the difficulty how all things heard of the Father can have been made known when many things are left unsaid a little later, answering that what is still to be done is spoken of as done.

outliers.claim: Raises the difficulty that all things heard of the Father are said to have been made known although many things are declared a little later to be unbearable and so unsaid, and answers that what is yet to be done is spoken of as already done, as the prophet wrote that they pierced his hands and feet rather than that they would

themes: This is my commandment, That ye love one another, as I have loved you.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Ye are my friends, if ye do whatsoever I command you.
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.

16.pericope_label: Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you. These things I command you, that ye love one another.

schools.summary: Ellicott warns that ordained has acquired a modern sense which misleads and would read appointed, and is careful that these things looks back rather than forward, the precepts having been given in order that they might love one another. Barnes presses the word chosen as the one from which election derives, takes it of their appointment as apostles, and draws out the disinterestedness of a love that began when they had no affection to offer, noting that what the older articles of religion called grace preventing a man means grace going before him. Robertson counts three present subjunctives in the purpose clause and makes them all insist on continuance rather than a spurt, and supplies the reason the command of love was needed that night, since the men hearing it had been quarrelling about precedence a few hours before. Lightfoot quotes the maxim of Joshua ben Perachiah, choose thyself a master and get thyself a colleague, to show the custom that is here reversed.

Gill notes the same Jewish custom of a disciple choosing his own teacher, adding the rabbinic tradition that made that teacher the master of Jesus of Nazareth, and counts this the third time love has been urged in these last discourses. Calvin takes the clause to claim for Christ alone what is usually divided between grace and the human will, since no one is moved of his own accord to seek him until he has been sought, grants that the immediate subject is the special calling to the apostolic office and argues from the lesser to the greater that the adoption common to believers is no less free, and narrows the command of mutual love to ministers, without which each labours apart and what rises is a heap rather than a building.

Clarke prefers I have placed you and reports the observation, taken from Wetstein, that Theodore of Mopsuestia treated the verb as meaning planted, so that the figure of the vine is still running, not merely planted but caused to spread through the habitable world. Wesley takes the going as conversion of sinners and the abiding fruit as lasting to the end of the world and beyond, and reads the promise about prayer as a consequence of the going rather than a separate gift.

Augustine identifies the fruit with love itself, which is why the apostle names love first among the fruits of the Spirit and treats the rest as springing from it, so that without it nothing profits and with it nothing is lacking to make a man good.

outliers.claim: Reports from Wetstein that Theodore of Mopsuestia took the verb rendered ordained to mean planted, keeping the figure of the vine alive in the verse, so that the apostles are not merely appointed but planted and made to spread through the habitable world

themes: Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
These things I command you, that ye love one another.

18.pericope_label: If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you. If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you. Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also. But all these things will they do unto you for my name’s sake, because they know not him that sent me.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the contrast between the love of the previous verse and the hatred of this, takes the opening verb as imperative so that the hatred itself becomes a bond with their Master, exposes the selfishness of the world's affection, which would love not them but whatever in them was its own, holds the English version of the remembered saying exact, and observes that Acts and the Epistles are one long commentary on the promise of persecution. Barnes points to the example of Jesus, whom no opposition deterred, and turns the hatred into a test, that a man may reckon the enmity of wicked men one evidence of his piety. Robertson treats the condition as assumed true, notes the perfect tense, has hated and hates still, turns the test on the reader by asking whether the world hates us and if not whether the world has grown more Christian or Christians more worldly, and remarks that the world praises the word of Jesus and dreads to follow it.

Gill takes the hatred for granted rather than supposed, since they had already had some experience of it. Calvin explains the warning as a precaution against raw recruits, valiant before they see an enemy and trembling once battle opens, states that the gospel cannot be published without driving the world to rage, makes the separation from the world the cause of its hatred while adding that they were once part of it and are distinguished only by mercy, reads the first verb of the remembered saying as imperative, and says no one would knowingly take the field against God, so it is blindness that hurries the world along.

Clarke passes on a suggestion of Lardner that the first word in the clause is a noun, so that the sense would run, know that it hated me, your Chief; he quotes a couplet of Gambold that the laws of Christ condemn a vicious world and goad it to revenge; he prefers a different sense for the verb in the remembered saying, that they watched his sayings with intent to accuse and will watch theirs likewise; and he draws a conclusion none of the others reach, that since persecution rests on ignorance of God those guilty of it in church or state know nothing of him, and where a worship troubles nobody's peace no man has the least right to meddle with it. Wesley reduces the world's enmity to the plain reason that the maxims, tempers and actions are opposite, and extends the verse to all ages and nations.

Henry makes hatred the genius of the devil's kingdom as love is of Christ's, and answers who is meant by the world in three ways: their number, with the dry remark that if it were put to a vote between Christ and Satan he fears Satan would out-poll us; their combination, since Jews and Gentiles who agreed in nothing else agreed in persecuting Christ's ministers; and their spirit, men wholly given to this world and never thinking of another.
Augustine notices what the others pass over, that in calling them servants here, so soon after saying he would call them servants no longer, the same speaker uses the word he had just withdrawn.

debates.question: What does the verb mean in if they have kept my saying?

positions.position: Kept, as the English version has it, the two clauses being joined because the word of Christ is the word of his disciples
Watched, with intent to accuse, which is far more agreeable to the context

outliers.claim: Argues from the verse that religious persecution rests on ignorance of God, so that those guilty of it in church or state know nothing of him, and that where a worship disturbs nobody the magistrate who meddles with it is fighting against God

themes: If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.
If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you.
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
But all these things will they do unto you for my name’s sake, because they know not him that sent me.

22.pericope_label: If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin. He that hateth me hateth my Father also. If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father. But this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause.

schools.summary: Ellicott puts the sin as a change of category, since apart from the revelation the fault would have belonged to the times of ignorance God overlooked, the negative evil of men who do not know, whereas now it is the positive evil of men who know and refuse; he traces the ascent from hatred of the disciples to hatred of the Son they represent and of the Father he represents, ending where it must, that a heart able to hate love has hardened past being loved; he notes how the evidence of the works was met, by calling him a sinner with a devil; and he thinks the sixty-ninth psalm the likeliest source of the quotation while noting the words stand also in the thirty-fifth. Barnes adds that the proof offered was argument as much as miracle and sorts the superiority of the works into number, kind, and the fact that prophets invoked a power this speaker simply used. Robertson notes that the word for excuse means a mere pretence and appears in John only here and two verses later, allows either psalm, takes law to stand for the whole of Scripture, and reads the perfect tenses as fixing a permanent attitude and responsibility. Lightfoot says briefly that the sin meant is rejecting the Messiah and refers forward to the next chapter's definition.

Gill lists the marks of authority that came with the speaking and the miracles that followed it. Calvin anticipates the objection that ignorance might excuse them, answering that the blindness is itself malicious, like a man shutting his eyes against the light, and that the Teacher did his duty without success because their malice would not let them be taught; on the works he reports the complaint that these miracles were neither more nor greater than those of Moses and the prophets, replies that Christ was not their minister but their author, then widens the word to cover every testimony of divine power in him; and he cites the thirty-fifth psalm to charge the nation with a malice running unbroken from grandfathers to grandchildren, observing that their law is said not out of respect but to wound.

Clarke renders the phrase without excuse and observes that both the sin and its consequence continue wherever the rejection does; he assigns the closing quotation to the sixty-ninth psalm and treats that psalm as prophetic throughout, mapping its verses onto the abasement, the garden, the crucifixion and what followed. Wesley refers the quotation to the same psalm without comment.

Augustine says the sin is not every sin but one great sin containing the rest and alone blocking forgiveness of the others, unbelief, so that the coming which saved the believing ruined the unbelieving; he raises the difficulty how men can hate a Father they are elsewhere said not to know, since either what they hate is something they have imagined, and then it is not God they hate, or they conceive him as he is and cannot be said not to know him; and on the works he grants that prophets raised the dead while denying that any healed so many infirmities, pressing the preposition, which means not among them but within them.

debates.question: Which psalm is quoted for hating without a cause?

positions.position: The sixty-ninth, which is prophetic of Christ throughout
Probably the sixty-ninth, though the words stand also in the thirty-fifth
The thirty-fifth
Either, law standing here for the whole of Scripture

debates.question: How were the works greater than those of Moses and the prophets?

positions.position: Christ was not the minister of them but their author, and the word covers every testimony of divine power in him
None of the prophets healed so many infirmities, and the works were done within them rather than merely among them, by his own power
They surpassed in number, in kind, and in being done by a power he used rather than invoked

outliers.claim: Asks how men can be said to hate the Father whom they are elsewhere said not to know, and frames the dilemma that either they hate something of their own imagining, which is not God, or they conceive him as he is and cannot be said to be ignorant of him

themes: If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin.
He that hateth me hateth my Father also.
If I had not done among them the works which none other man did, they had not had sin: but now have they both seen and hated both me and my Father.
But this cometh to pass, that the word might be fulfilled that is written in their law, They hated me without a cause.

26.pericope_label: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me: And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.

schools.summary: Ellicott prefers Advocate to Comforter, notes the emphatic pronoun, and treats three descriptions as one act, the mission by the Father at the Son's asking, in the Son's name, and by the Son himself, taking the clause about proceeding from the Father to lend the witness the Father's own weight; on the apostolic testimony he points out that the tense is present, so they already are witnesses, that the apostles distinguished their own testimony from the Spirit's, and that the beginning means the beginning of the Messianic work. Barnes states the qualification plainly, that more than three years of observation fitted them to speak of his character and doctrine. Robertson calls the verse the Procession of the Spirit from the Father and from the Son, observes that the neuter relative should be rendered who and that the pronoun following is emphatic and masculine though its antecedent is neuter, and ends with a rebuke, that this is the point at which Christians fail most.

Gill sets out the Advocate's work most fully: pleading against the world, reproving it of sin and righteousness and judgment, assisting the disciples before princes, and comforting them by applying the things of Christ, shedding abroad the love of God, applying the promises, witnessing their adoption and sealing them. Calvin turns to the effect on the hearer, that a truth sealed by the Spirit on the heart can despise whatever the world raises against it, whereas a faith resting on the opinions of men would be overwhelmed a hundred times a day; and he insists the gift was not for the apostles' private benefit but for wide diffusion, using the pairing of Spirit and preaching against two errors at once, those who think faith is produced by preaching alone and the fanatics who despise outward preaching and talk loftily of secret inspirations.

Clarke reads the promise as the last step in an argument about inexcusable unbelief, the doctrine being pure and the mission confirmed by miracles, so that one thing only remained, to send the Spirit who would convince them; and he lists the means by which the apostles bore their witness, their miracles, preaching, writings, lives and deaths. Wesley argues that coming, being sent and testifying are personal acts which distinguish the Spirit from both Father and Son, that the title and the procession can belong to none but a divine person, and that procession from the Son may be fairly argued from his being called the Spirit of Christ and from his being sent by the Son.

Henry claims that this verse tells us more of the Holy Spirit than any other single verse in the Bible, insists the language describes a distinct person rather than a quality or property, adds that when Christ was reviled he committed his cause to his Father and lost nothing by silence since the Advocate came and pleaded it powerfully, and divides the support of the cause into the principal testimony of the Spirit and the subordinate testimony of the apostles.

Chrysostom frames the paragraph as an answer to an unspoken objection: if men who heard such words and saw such works were not convinced but hated both the Son and the Father, what hope have envoys of being believed? The reply is that another witness is coming.

Augustine sharpens the contrast, that seeing him they hated and killed him while the Advocate will testify so that men believe without seeing, and explains that the disciples do not yet speak boldly because they lack the fulness of the Spirit, who will take fear from his friends and turn the hatred of his enemies into love.

outliers.claim: Claims that this single verse tells us more concerning the Holy Ghost than any other verse in the Bible, and treats it as the warrant for knowing the Spirit as a distinct person rather than a quality or property

themes: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
And ye also shall bear witness, because ye have been with me from the beginning.
